name: Pulmonary valve
func: A three-cusp one-way valve at the exit of the right ventricle. It opens to let oxygen-poor blood flow into the pulmonary trunk toward the lungs, then closes so it can't flow back into the heart.

levels.kid:
The right side of your heart sends tired, used-up blood to your lungs so it can pick up fresh air. To get there, the blood leaves the bottom-right room through a door called the **pulmonary valve**. "Pulmonary" means "about the lungs."

The door has three small cup-shaped flaps. When the room squeezes, the cups lie flat and blood whooshes out toward the lungs. When the squeeze stops, the cups fill up and close together, like three hands meeting in a high-five, so no blood can slip back.

It's the door closest to the front of your chest.
levels.hs:
The **pulmonary valve** sits at the top of the **right ventricle**, at the end of a smooth funnel called the **conus arteriosus (infundibulum)**, and opens into the **pulmonary trunk**. It is the most **anterior and superior** of the four valves, lying behind the left side of the sternum near the **left third costal cartilage**, just in front of and to the left of the aortic valve.

Like the aortic valve, it is a **semilunar valve** with three cusps (usually named **anterior, left and right**) and no chordae tendineae. Its cusps are thinner than the aortic valve's because pressures on the right side of the heart are much lower.

It opens during **ventricular systole** and closes at the start of diastole, contributing to the **second heart sound (S2)**. On breathing in, more blood returns to the right heart, so the pulmonary valve closes slightly later than the aortic valve. This produces a normal **physiological splitting of S2** that a doctor can hear at the **left upper sternal border** (2nd intercostal space).
levels.college:
The pulmonary valve differs from the aortic valve in a key structural way: it is supported by a complete **muscular infundibulum** (subpulmonary conus), so there is **no fibrous continuity** with the tricuspid valve, whereas the aortic valve touches the mitral valve directly. This muscular sleeve lifts the pulmonary valve higher and further forward.

That muscle can be harvested: in the **Ross procedure**, surgeons move the patient's own pulmonary valve into the aortic position and replace the pulmonary valve with a donor (homograft) valve. The living autograft can grow, which makes the operation attractive for children and young adults.

The **left main coronary artery** passes immediately behind the pulmonary trunk, an important relation during root surgery.

S2 splitting: the aortic component (A2) normally precedes the pulmonary component (P2). Splitting widens on inspiration. **Wide fixed splitting** suggests an **atrial septal defect**; **paradoxical (reversed) splitting**, where the split appears in expiration, suggests delayed LV emptying, such as **left bundle branch block** or severe aortic stenosis. A **loud P2** suggests **pulmonary hypertension**.

Peak pressure across a normal valve is low, around 25 mmHg in the RV; a gradient of tens of mmHg indicates stenosis.
levels.phd:
Developmentally, the outflow valves (aortic and pulmonary) arise from the **outflow tract cushions**, colonized by both endocardially derived mesenchyme and **cardiac neural crest cells**, and their arterial walls derive in part from the **second heart field**. Septation of the common outflow tract by the spiraling **aorticopulmonary septum** produces the characteristic twisting of the great arteries around each other.

Disruption of neural crest migration or second heart field contribution causes a family of **conotruncal defects**: **tetralogy of Fallot**, **truncus arteriosus** and **double-outlet right ventricle**. These are strongly associated with **22q11.2 deletion syndrome** (TBX1 haploinsufficiency), which also affects the thymus and parathyroids.

In **tetralogy of Fallot**, anterior and leftward deviation of the outlet septum narrows the subpulmonary outflow, producing pulmonary stenosis, a ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta and RV hypertrophy.

Isolated **pulmonary valve stenosis** is often caused by a dome-shaped valve with fused commissures; a **dysplastic** thickened valve is characteristic of **Noonan syndrome** (RAS–MAPK pathway mutations such as PTPN11). Because the RV is thin-walled and compliant, it tolerates chronic **pulmonary regurgitation** for years, but eventually dilates, and RV volume on MRI is used to time valve replacement.

Tissue-engineered and decellularized pulmonary valves are an active research area, since the low-pressure position is a forgiving testbed for growing valves.
levels.expert:
**Pulmonary stenosis** gives an **ejection systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border**, often with an **ejection click** that softens on inspiration (the only right-sided sound that does), a delayed, soft P2 and a prominent jugular **a wave** from RV hypertrophy. **Pulmonary regurgitation** gives an early diastolic murmur at the same spot; when it is due to pulmonary hypertension it is called a **Graham Steell murmur**.

Most clinically significant pulmonary valve disease is **congenital**. Many adults with repaired **tetralogy of Fallot** develop severe pulmonary regurgitation decades after their childhood repair and need lifelong follow-up for RV dilation, arrhythmias and sudden death risk.

Acquired causes include **carcinoid** heart disease and endocarditis (rarely isolated).

Imaging: echo measures the gradient and regurgitation; **cardiac MRI** is the reference standard for RV volumes and regurgitant fraction; CT maps the coronary arteries before catheter procedures because a stent frame can compress a nearby coronary.

Treatment in general terms: **balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty** is first-line for typical stenosis and often curative. Pulmonary regurgitation is treated by surgical valve replacement or, increasingly, by **transcatheter pulmonary valve implantation**, threaded up from a leg vein through the right heart, avoiding repeat open-heart surgery.

keyPoints: Exit valve of the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk
Most anterior and superior heart valve
Heard best at the left upper sternal border
P2 closes after A2; splitting widens with inspiration
Used as the autograft in the Ross procedure

test.q: The pulmonary valve opens into the:
test.explain: Blood leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, which splits into the pulmonary arteries.

test.q: Which is the most anterior of the four heart valves?
test.explain: The pulmonary valve sits highest and furthest forward, atop the muscular infundibulum.

test.q: Wide FIXED splitting of S2 classically suggests an atrial ______ defect.
test.explain: In an ASD, shunting keeps right-sided volume high in both phases of breathing, so the split doesn't change.

test.q: The operation that moves a patient's own pulmonary valve into the aortic position is the ______ procedure.
test.explain: The autograft can grow, which suits children; a donor valve replaces the pulmonary valve.

test.q: Severe pulmonary regurgitation decades later is a typical problem after repair of:
test.explain: Repairing the RV outflow in Fallot often sacrifices the valve, so regurgitation and RV dilation follow.
